greeting.text: The woman at the small desk inside the door of Number Nine finishes the line she is writing before she looks up, and then gives you her whole attention, which is considerable. "Minna Crale. I keep the book." She turns the agenda round so you can read it: the dividend; the Greyhythe return; the water rights; any other business. "You've come down from the valley. You'll have business. The meeting will be very glad to hear it, if it's in order. What is it?"

interjections.text: Sera reads the agenda upside down, faster than you read it the right way up.

choices.label: I have the survey. All nine sheets.
I'm here about the survey that burned.
I'm on the house's books. Corse retains us.
Rivermark heard sheet six read aloud. I've come about that.

greeting.text: Minna Crale reads something on a slip of paper that came up the stairs before you did, and inks your name on the agenda, over the pencil. "In order," she says. "Item seven, after the water rights. They're sitting now. Go up, and speak when Mr Sare looks at you. He will."

Minna Crale takes a folded paper from a pigeonhole that has your name on a card, in her hand. "Your first instruction under the articles," she says. "It's quite short." It is. It says: Attend the quarterly meeting. If asked, say whether the valley is quiet. It is initialled by somebody, and countersigned by somebody else.

interjections.text: Aldric reads it twice and gives it back to you as though it were wet.
Sera: "That's the whole service. They're paying for the sentence."

choices.label: Then I'll say it. The valley is quiet.
Where's the clause for ending it?
Here's your forty back. The articles are void.

greeting.text: "Still in pencil," Minna Crale says, not unkindly, tapping your line on the agenda. "I'll ink it when it's in order. The meeting does not hear things twice, so it's a kindness to hear them once, properly."
"They're sitting," Minna Crale says, and nods at the stair. "Item seven. Go up."

Minna Crale has a slip of paper ready, which means she has had it ready for some time. "Before you go," she says. "The Greyhythe office has a line in its book against your party. Service given: a list of forty-one names, copied. Service owed: and then a blank, where the day would be." She lays the slip on the desk. "The house would like the day to be today. It is a very small service. I would not want you to think otherwise."

interjections.text: Kessa goes very still, the way she does in doorways.

greeting.text: Minna Crale looks up, and something that is not quite a smile happens and is filed. "It's in the minutes," she says. "Whatever you said. Everything is. That's what I'm for."
"Number Nine," Minna Crale says. "If you've business with the meeting, Mr Moss at the yard will tell you how it's done. It isn't difficult. That's rather the point of it."

the_eleven.text: "Subscribers," she says. "The articles allow twelve. There have been eleven since Mrs Orme died; the twelfth share is lapsed and may be taken up on payment of the call. Two banks, a ship-owner, a man who makes rope, three widows, a clergyman, a family that has been in it since the beginning, and two I've never met, who vote by letter." She considers. "They're not wicked. I've sat in the corner for eleven years and they're not. They read the figures. They ask whether the figures are right. They usually are."

interjections.text: Kessa: "A man who makes rope." Minna Crale: "Very good rope."

matter_took.text: Minna Crale looks at the oilcloth packet without reaching for it. "That's a survey," she says. "A fair copy. The meeting won't read it, I'm afraid. It reads the field books, and the field books are in the Record Office, three doors down, filed. Corse would have told you." She makes a pencil note. "Have Mrs Fenn put them beside your sheets. Then come back, and I'll know what your matter actually is."

matter_burned.text: "Ah," Minna Crale says, and her pencil stops. "Then there's an open return against it. A gentleman came back down this morning with it, on your boat. He's at the Fortieth, being unwell." She chooses the next words. "The meeting can't hear a matter while a return is open on it. Mr Pellow would very much like to close it. You might help each other."

matter_sold.text: "You are," Minna Crale says, and she does not look anything up. "Forty a quarter, the first lodged. There's an instruction for you; it came down with you. I'll fetch it." She is already standing. "It's the first one. They're always short."

matter_warned.text: "Yes," she says. "We had the return from Greyhythe. Three conveyances on Granary Row since the reading, at the old figure, and the rest asking." She says it the way she said the agenda. "The meeting will want the name of whoever read it out, for the minute. I have the name. He came down on your boat. He's at the Fortieth. I thought you might want to see him before he's minuted."

interjections.text: Aldric takes his hat off, and then seems not to know why, and puts it back on.

sold_serving.text: "Thank you," Minna Crale says, and writes will attend against your name, and then counts forty gold onto the desk. "The second quarter. In advance; I find it saves a letter." She does not wait to see what your face does. "Mr Sare will ask you. He always asks."

sold_clause.text: Minna Crale puts her pen down. You get the impression this happens about once a year. "There isn't one," she says. "Nobody has ever asked." She looks at the articles for a long moment, then takes a fresh sheet. "Either party. A quarter's notice. In writing, to Number Nine." She writes it out, fair, signs it as secretary, and pins it to your articles. "There. Now there is."

interjections.text: Ilse lets out a breath she has been holding since Greyhythe.

sold_returned.text: Minna Crale counts the forty, twice, and writes you a receipt in the same hand as the articles, and then files the receipt with the articles, so that they sit together in the same pigeonhole. "Mr Corse will be told," she says. "He won't be surprised. He's never been surprised by anybody, as far as I know. It must be very restful."

favour_what.text: "A witness," Minna Crale says. "Forty-one conveyances from the valley, signed by mark. The law wants it witnessed that each was read aloud to the seller before the mark was made. They were. Mr Corse is scrupulous about it." She turns the slip so you can read it. "The house would like a party who has walked the valley to sign that it has seen the record of the reading. Your name, here. That is all."

interjections.text: Kessa, flat: "Read aloud. They read mine aloud too. In a hurry, with a man waiting for the table."
Sera: "It is a perfectly ordinary attestation. That is the worst thing I can say about it."

choices.label: Read them aloud again. Here. All forty-one. Then I'll sign.
No. Leave the blank where it is.

favour_signed.text: You sign. Minna Crale blots it, and enters a line in a book you have not seen before, and draws a neat rule under the Greyhythe office's blank. "Discharged," she says. "Thank you. It really was very small." It was. That is what it was for.

favour_read.text:
Minna Crale looks at you for a moment, and then she gets up and fetches the bundle herself, and reads. All forty-one. It takes the whole of the afternoon and the fire has to be made up twice. Every conveyance is exactly what the seller was told it was. Kessa stands at the window with her back to the room and listens to every name.

When it is done you sign. Minna Crale blots it. "Nobody has ever asked for that," she says. "It was perfectly lawful the first time." She draws the rule. "It was better the second."

favour_refused.text: "It will keep," Minna Crale says, and puts the slip back in its pigeonhole, under your name. "Favours do. That is rather the point of them." She is not offended. She is never offended. Somewhere a line in a book in Greyhythe stays open, with a blank where the day would be.
